title: Tokenization — 7 Learning Questions
subtitle: Topic: Text Processing and Token Representation · Subject: Natural Language Processing (NLP). Seven supplied questions, four equally plausible choices, visual lessons, beginner explanations and optional technical detail.
hero:
TOKENIZATION · VISUAL OVERVIEW

Language enters as text; the model receives token IDs.

Tokens can be full words or smaller pieces. The tokenizer's vocabulary decides where the boundaries go.

questions.stem: What is Tokenization in Natural Language Processing (NLP), and why must text be divided into smaller units called tokens before it can be processed by language models?
options: It rewrites every sentence into simpler English before a language model begins processing the message.
It divides text into smaller units that a language model can turn into numeric inputs.
It removes rare words from sentences so the model only reads common vocabulary items.
It labels each sentence as positive or negative before any neural network performs calculations.
questions.explanation: In simple words: Tokenization cuts text into manageable pieces. The model turns those pieces into numbers so it can process the message.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: B. Tokenization breaks raw text into smaller units called tokens. An LLM cannot directly run attention over raw text characters. Its tokenizer uses a defined vocabulary to map tokens to numeric IDs, which the model uses to look up vectors. Tokens can be whole words, subwords, characters, or byte-derived pieces depending on the tokenizer.
questions.figure:
MEANING CUT LINE

A sentence becomes small pieces a model can number

Tokenization divides text first. A vocabulary then maps each token to a number the model can use.

questions.stem: How can a simple sentence such as "I love artificial intelligence" be divided into words, subwords, or individual characters, and why might different tokenizers split the same sentence differently?
options: Every tokenizer must split the same sentence into identical whole words regardless of training data.
Character tokenizers always produce fewer tokens than subword tokenizers for most ordinary English sentences.
A subword tokenizer must preserve every original word as one token whenever possible in practice.
Different tokenizers choose words, word pieces, or characters based on their vocabularies and rules.
questions.explanation: In simple words: A tokenizer might keep whole words or break them into smaller pieces. Different vocabularies produce different splits for the same sentence.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: D. For “I love artificial intelligence,” a simple whitespace tokenizer might produce four tokens. A subword tokenizer may split “intelligence” into smaller pieces, and a character tokenizer may split every character. Every tokenizer has its own vocabulary, preprocessing, normalization, and algorithm. Illustrated boundaries are examples rather than exact output from a specific pretrained tokenizer.
questions.figure:
THREE CUTTING STRATEGIES

One sentence, three ways to split

The pictured subword split is illustrative. Real boundaries depend on the trained tokenizer and its vocabulary.

questions.stem: What happens when a user enters a sentence into a Large Language Model (LLM), and how does the tokenizer convert the original text into tokens, assign numerical token IDs, and prepare them for processing by the model?
options: The tokenizer splits text, looks up token IDs, then passes those IDs toward the model.
The tokenizer creates final word embeddings and predicts the next response without using model layers.
The tokenizer searches the internet for numeric labels before sending the user sentence to attention.
The tokenizer permanently replaces unseen words with the same ID used for every punctuation mark.
questions.explanation: In simple words: The tokenizer splits your sentence and gives each piece an ID. The model then converts those IDs into vectors it can process.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: A. The tokenizer prepares raw text and converts it into vocabulary pieces and numeric IDs. A model uses its input embedding table to map those IDs into vectors. Depending on the model, tokenization may insert special IDs such as start or end markers and produce an attention mask. Token IDs are vocabulary-specific, so different tokenizers can assign different IDs to the same string.
questions.figure:
TOKEN ID ASSEMBLY LINE

From a typed sentence to token IDs and vectors

The IDs here are illustrative. Tokenizers assign IDs; the model's embedding layer creates vectors.

questions.stem: How do Word-Level, Character-Level, and Subword Tokenization methods differ, and how do algorithms such as Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), WordPiece, and Unigram Tokenization build vocabularies and handle unfamiliar words, rare terms, and multilingual text?
options: BPE, WordPiece, and Unigram all use identical frequency merges and the same finished vocabulary.
Character models need a vocabulary of full sentences, while word models avoid vocabulary lookup entirely.
BPE merges frequent pairs; WordPiece scores merges; Unigram prunes a candidate vocabulary of pieces.
Unigram uses only whole words, while BPE and WordPiece split all input into single characters.
questions.explanation: In simple words: Word tokenizers keep words, character tokenizers split letters, and subword methods learn reusable pieces. Their vocabulary-building rules differ.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: C. Word-level tokenization uses full words but struggles with unseen words. Character-level tokenization uses a smaller base alphabet but creates longer sequences. Byte Pair Encoding learns frequent neighboring merges; WordPiece scores candidate merges; Unigram starts with many candidate pieces and removes those contributing least. Unicode-aware and byte-level approaches help with rare or multilingual text. Hugging Face algorithm comparison.
questions.figure:
VOCABULARY WORKSHOP

How three subword algorithms learn pieces

Word-level uses whole words; character-level splits characters. BPE, WordPiece and Unigram learn subword vocabularies.

questions.stem: How can Tokenization be implemented and explored using Python and Hugging Face Tokenizers, including loading a pretrained tokenizer, encoding text into token IDs, decoding tokens back into text, handling special tokens, and comparing token counts across different sentences?
options: Load a tokenizer, then compare raw character counts without inspecting tokens or decoding their IDs.
Load a pretrained tokenizer, encode text, inspect token IDs, decode, and compare token counts.
Train a transformer from zero before a Python tokenizer can encode any English sentence reliably.
Count the words in Python, then use those word counts as the model vocabulary IDs.
questions.explanation: In simple words: In Python, load a tokenizer, turn text into IDs, inspect the pieces, and decode them. Compare counts to see different splits.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: B. With Hugging Face Transformers, AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased") loads a tokenizer. tokenizer(text) returns input IDs and masks, convert_ids_to_tokens shows pieces, and decode(ids, skip_special_tokens=True) reconstructs normalized text. BERT inserts [CLS] and [SEP] in this use case. Lowercasing and normalizing can mean decoded text differs from the original.
questions.figure:
PYTHON TOKEN LAB

Inspect real token IDs with a pretrained Python tokenizer

tokenization_example.py Hugging Face · Python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

# Downloads the pretrained tokenizer once
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(
    "bert-base-uncased", use_fast=True
)
text = "Hello, world!"
encoded = tok(text)
ids = encoded["input_ids"]
pieces = tok.convert_ids_to_tokens(ids)
restored = tok.decode(ids, skip_special_tokens=True)
print(pieces, ids, restored)

texts = ["Hi", "Artificial intelligence"]
print([len(tok(t)["input_ids"]) for t in texts])

The pictured tokens match this illustrative BERT example; actual IDs and output come from the loaded tokenizer.

questions.stem: How do tokenizer vocabulary size, token granularity, byte-level encoding, Unicode handling, and special tokens influence the efficiency and behavior of Transformer-based LLMs, particularly when processing code, numbers, multilingual languages, and long documents?
options: Vocabulary and byte-handling choices change token counts, special-token behavior, and efficiency across scripts.
Unicode always maps one character to one token, even with byte-level or subword tokenization.
A larger vocabulary guarantees fewer attention operations without increasing the model's embedding storage requirements.
Code, multilingual text, and numbers use identical token counts whenever their character lengths match.
questions.explanation: In simple words: The same text can use more or fewer tokens depending on the tokenizer. That changes memory use, sequence length, and cost.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: A. Smaller vocabularies often produce more tokens per input; larger vocabularies require larger embedding and sometimes output tables. Byte-level encodings can handle unseen Unicode, though a single character can use multiple bytes and tokens. Programming whitespace, numbers, multilingual scripts and special tokens are not guaranteed to use the same number of tokens even when character counts match.
questions.figure:
UNICODE VOCABULARY LENS

Token size changes with language, code and bytes

One Unicode character can occupy multiple UTF-8 bytes. Fewer vocabulary entries often mean longer token sequences.

questions.stem: How does Tokenization affect the training and inference costs of Large Language Models, including context-window utilization, sequence length, memory consumption, attention computation, and token generation speed, and what challenges arise when modifying a tokenizer or extending its vocabulary after a model has already been pretrained?
options: Doubling tokens only doubles full attention work, and vocabulary edits leave old model weights compatible.
More tokens reduce memory automatically, while new vocabulary entries never need training or embedding updates.
Context windows count words, not tokens, so tokenizer choice cannot affect training or inference costs.
Token counts affect context and compute; vocabulary changes require matching and training new model embeddings.
questions.explanation: In simple words: More tokens fill the context window faster and increase attention work. Changing vocabulary also means updating and training matching model embeddings.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: D. Context windows count tokens rather than words. In standard dense full attention, doubling sequence length yields roughly four times the attention-score work at the same hidden dimensions. KV caching changes generation costs but does not eliminate long-context memory needs. Changing a tokenizer can change token IDs; model embedding and output layers may need resizing or retraining, and compatible old mappings must be preserved.
questions.figure:
CONTEXT COST BENCHMARK

Double the sequence length → about four times dense attention work

For standard dense attention, cost grows roughly with token count squared. Cache and architecture change actual inference costs.
